content: If left untreated, patients with lymphatic filariasis may develop chronic lymphedema, hydrocele, skin pigmentation changes, and chyluria. The prognosis is generally favorable in early cases, but in chronic cases, the disease can result in severe disability, including genital damage. Lymphatic filariasis can present as either asymptomatic or symptomatic. Symptomatic cases may include acute adenolymphangitis, filarial fever, and tropical pulmonary eosinophilia. If untreated, the disease can progress to lymphatic dilation, abnormalities in lymphatic drainage, and microscopic hematuria and proteinuria. Complications associated with lymphatic filariasis include the following: Lymphedema: This refers to non-pitting edema in the limbs caused by chronic inflammation and obstruction of lymphatic vessels. Lymphedema commonly affects the upper limbs and may involve the breasts, particularly in areas endemic to Wuchereria bancrofti. Hydrocele: This condition involves significant swelling of the genitalia due to lymphatic obstruction, with some cases reporting hydroceles up to 30 cm in diameter. This can predispose individuals to bacterial infections. Additionally, cases of filariasis affecting the ovary and mesosalpinx have been reported. Renal involvement: Increased intestinal lymph drainage into renal vessels can lead to the loss of lymphatic fluid in the urine, giving it a milky appearance, a condition known as chyluria. In terms of prognosis, early or mild cases of filariasis, including acute inflammatory episodes, typically respond well to treatment. The disease can be managed and progression prevented with simple measures such as maintaining hygiene, proper skin care, regular exercise, and elevation of affected limbs. However, chronic infections are less responsive to these interventions. While filariasis rarely results in mortality, it can cause significant disability, including genital damage or elephantiasis. Lymphatic filariasis is the second leading cause of disability worldwide, with approximately 40 million individuals suffering from complications that impair occupational activities, limit educational and employment opportunities, and reduce mobility.
